What you will see are the traces of an older Iceland: turf-roofed ruins, drying racks for fish and rusting winches on the quay. In the quiet hours of a summer night, the light makes everything look gilded, and the sea has a metallic sheen.
t.diamond circle point 2@66.0,-16.5:
Ásbyrgi is a canyon shaped like a horseshoe, about a kilometre wide and three and a half long, with cliffs rising up to a hundred metres and a forest of birch and willow growing on its floor. It feels like a hidden world, sheltered from the wind, green and quiet, and after the open, rugged landscape around it the effect is almost startling. A rocky island stands in the middle, dividing the canyon's head.

The old story says that the canyon is the hoofprint of Sleipnir, the eight-legged horse of Odin, who touched down here on his flight across the sky. The scientific story is more dramatic: geologists believe that enormous floods of glacial meltwater, released from beneath the ice cap in catastrophic bursts thousands of years ago, tore the canyon from the rock, and the Jökulsá river, which once flowed here, later shifted its course to the east. Either story is worth thinking about as you stand at the head of the canyon.

The road in from the main route is easy and the surface good. The canyon is part of the great national park along the Jökulsá river, which also includes Dettifoss, and the landscape here is a mixture of lava, sand and scrub. Wind can be fierce on the open plain, but inside the canyon it is calm. Traffic is generally light, and the approach has long views of the Arctic horizon.

Nature is the great attraction. The birch forest is one of the few in the north, and in summer it is full of birdsong, with redwings and wrens, and sometimes even ravens and falcons nesting on the cliffs. There are walking paths, a pond at the head of the canyon, and a campsite with a visitor centre near the entrance.

Services near the canyon are limited to the visitor centre and campsite, with a shop and a cafe, but Húsavík is the nearest town of any size. Allow an hour or two for a walk, and go in the morning if you can.
t.diamond circle point 3@65.8,-16.4:
Dettifoss makes a noise you can feel in your sternum before you see anything. The waterfall on the Jökulsá á Fjöllum is forty-four metres high and about a hundred wide, and it carries more water than any other in Europe, a grey, thundering mass of glacial silt and ice melt that drops into a canyon of black basalt. In summer the flow can reach several hundred cubic metres per second, and the spray rises in clouds that catch rainbows on sunny days.

Getting here is half the adventure. The approach from the Ring Road to the west side is generally paved, while the eastern approach is gravel and rougher, so choose according to your bike and your nerves, and check the conditions before setting out. The surrounding landscape is a vast, barren plain of lava and black sand, almost lunar in its emptiness, with the wind scouring everything and the temperature dropping fast. Roads can be closed by snow well into early summer.

The landscape has the feel of another planet, and it was chosen as the opening scene of a science fiction film in 2012, set on a primeval Earth. The river that feeds the falls rises under the great Vatnajökull ice cap and carries its sediment northward to the sea, grinding through the plateau as it goes. A few kilometres upstream is a smaller fall, Selfoss, and downstream is the dramatic gorge of Hafragilsfoss, with its basalt columns.

Nature here is spare and strong. The vegetation is thin, mostly moss and hardy grasses, and the air carries a mineral smell from the spray. In early summer, pink-footed geese and other birds pass through, and the occasional Arctic fox shows itself on the ridges. The colours are dominated by black, grey and white, until a rainbow breaks them.

There are only basic facilities, and nothing in the way of shops, so Húsavík and the Mývatn area are the main places for supplies. Walk the path to the edge of the gorge, keep well back from the edge, and give yourself time to watch.
t.diamond circle point 4@65.6,-17.0:
Mývatn means midge lake, and the name is not a joke. In summer the lake is alive with small flies that rise in clouds from the water, a delight for the trout and the ducks and a nuisance for visitors, who learn quickly to carry a head net. In return, the lake is one of the richest bird habitats in Europe, with more species of duck breeding here than almost anywhere, and it sits in a landscape so strange that you start to doubt which planet you are on.

The ride around the lake is a series of surprises. The road is generally good, with gentle bends, and passes through lava fields and past strange formations. Dimmuborgir, the dark castles, is a maze of twisted lava pillars and caves, said in folklore to be the home of trolls and the Yule Lads. At Hverir, a barren field of boiling mud pots and steaming vents, the ground is stained yellow with sulphur, and the smell is powerful. The Krafla volcanic area, where eruptions continued through the early eighties, is nearby.

The lake itself was formed by a huge volcanic eruption about two thousand years ago, and it is dotted with pseudocraters, formed when lava flowed over wet ground and the steam blasted holes. The shallow, warm water supports a rich ecosystem, and the lake is a nature reserve. A geothermal bathing lagoon nearby is a good way to ease sore muscles after the ride.

Nature is exceptional. Besides the ducks, the area is famed for its rich plant life, with mosses, lichens and flowers thriving on the lava, and the long summer evenings give a soft, golden light across the water. The smell of sulphur and wet earth is constant.

The villages around the lake have shops, cafes and places to stay, and it is a good base for a night or two. Be prepared for the midges, and ride in the morning or evening to avoid the worst. Wind can be strong, and the air is cold, even in summer.
t.near lat bua luang on the way back@14.2,:
Rice fields stretch flat to the horizon here, in the Central Plain of Thailand northwest of Bangkok, broken only by canals, villages on stilts, temples with glittering roofs and lines of palms. This point lies near Lat Bua Luang, a district in Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya province, in the fertile, low-lying country between the Chao Phraya and Tha Chin rivers, where water shapes almost everything about daily life.

This is the heartland of old Siam. Ayutthaya, the capital of the kingdom for four centuries until it was sacked by the Burmese in 1767, lies a short ride to the northeast, and its ruined temples and brick stupas, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are among the most impressive sights in Thailand. The canals around here were dug for irrigation and transport, and many villages still have houses facing the water, with boats tied to the steps.

As for the swim, honesty first: the canals and rivers here are working waterways, muddy and full of boat traffic, and they are not a good idea for swimming. Some resorts and hotels have pools, and local water parks exist on the outskirts of Bangkok, but in the middle of the rice country, a cooling stop is more likely to mean a cold drink and some shade at a roadside stall than a plunge.

The roads in this area are flat and mostly straight, crossing the plain between towns and villages, with occasional bridges over canals. Traffic varies from quiet country lanes to busy highways full of trucks and buses. Watch for dogs, scooters coming the wrong way, and sudden potholes. Thailand drives on the left. In the hot season, from March to May, temperatures can exceed thirty-five degrees Celsius, and in the rainy season, from roughly June to October, heavy afternoon storms flood roads quickly.

Fuel stations are common along the main roads, often with small shops and coffee stalls, and the nearest larger town is Bang Len, about twenty kilometres away. Food is everywhere: noodle soups, grilled pork and sticky rice, fresh fruit and iced drinks from roadside stalls. Drink plenty of water and take breaks in the shade on the long, hot ride back toward Bangkok.
t.samut sakhon@13.5,100.3:
Samut Sakhon smells of the sea. The city sits at the mouth of the Tha Chin River where it flows into the Gulf of Thailand, about thirty kilometres southwest of Bangkok, and it has been a fishing port for centuries. Locals often still call it Mahachai, its old name. Boats crowd the river, and the fish market near the pier is one of the busiest in the country, piled with prawns, squid, crabs and fish of every kind.

Around the city, the flat coastal land is crisscrossed by canals and dotted with salt pans and shrimp farms. Along the road to the west you can see workers raking salt into white heaps in the evaporation ponds, a tradition that goes back generations. Samut Sakhon also has a large community of migrant workers from Myanmar, many working in the seafood processing industry, and their presence gives parts of the city a distinctive character, with Burmese shops and food.

One of the most unusual ways to arrive is by train. The Maeklong Railway runs from Bangkok to Mahachai, where passengers take a ferry across the river and then another train continues to the famous market at Maeklong, where vendors pull back their awnings as the train passes through the stalls.

About the swim: the coast here is mud flats and mangroves rather than beaches, and the water is brown, shallow and used by fishing boats. Not a place for swimming. If you want a beach, the resorts of Hua Hin or Pattaya are a long ride away. Here, the best way to cool off is a cold drink at a seafood restaurant overlooking the river or the sea.

Riding in Samut Sakhon is busy and flat. The Rama II Road, the main highway southwest from Bangkok, is crowded with trucks and buses, and the city streets are full of scooters, pickups and street vendors. Traffic can be chaotic, with sudden lane changes and vehicles entering without warning. Fuel and food are everywhere. Try the seafood, especially grilled prawns, steamed crabs and fried fish, at one of the many restaurants by the water, then head back toward Ayutthaya and the river roads.
t.kampot@10.6,104.2:
Kampot is a lazy river town on the southern coast of Cambodia, and it wears its faded French colonial architecture with a sort of gentle indifference. Old shophouses with peeling yellow paint and wooden shutters line the riverfront, and the wide Preaek Tuek Chhu river flows slowly past, with fishing boats heading out to sea in the evening. Across the river, the bulk of Bokor Mountain rises over the town, often wrapped in cloud. It is a place where people come for a few days and stay for weeks.

The town is famous for its pepper. Kampot pepper has been grown in the area for centuries and was prized by French chefs in colonial times; after decades of neglect during the Khmer Rouge years and their aftermath, the plantations were revived and the pepper now carries a protected geographical indication. You can visit farms in the countryside around town and taste green, black, red and white pepper, all from the same vine. The salt flats east of town, where seawater is evaporated in shallow pans, are another local industry worth a look.

Kampot is also a good base for exploring the coast. The small seaside town of Kep, about twenty kilometres away, is known for its crab market, where crabs are cooked with fresh green pepper, and its once-grand villas, many of them left ruined after the war. The countryside between Kampot and Kep is flat and green, with rice fields, palm trees and limestone hills with caves and temples hidden inside.

For riders, Kampot is the starting point for the climb up Bokor, and the town has everything you need: fuel, mechanics, guesthouses, cafes and restaurants serving everything from Khmer curries to pizza. The roads in town are often chaotic, with motorbikes, tuk-tuks and trucks all competing for space, and the traffic rules are flexible, to put it mildly. November to April is the dry season and the easy time to come, with dusty but dry roads. The rainy season brings heavy afternoon downpours and humidity, but also lush green landscapes and fewer tourists.
t.near kampot@10.6,104.1:
At the foot of Bokor, west of Kampot, the land is flat and green, and then suddenly it isn't. The mountain rises abruptly from the coastal plain, a long ridge of sandstone covered in dense forest, and the road up begins with almost no warning, leaving the rice paddies and palm trees behind and starting to climb. Here is the entrance to Preah Monivong Bokor National Park, and the beginning of one of the best mountain roads in Cambodia.

The road was originally built by the French in the 1920s to reach a hill station on the plateau, a place where colonial officials could escape the heat of the lowlands. It was a remarkable feat of engineering, and it came at a cost: many of the labourers who built it are said to have died from disease and accidents. The old road fell into ruin during the decades of war, and the modern road, rebuilt in recent years as part of a development project on the plateau, is wide, smooth and well engineered, a pleasure to ride.

The climb is about thirty kilometres long and rises to around a thousand metres, with long, flowing curves, a few hairpins and constant views back over the coast. On a clear day you can see the Gulf of Thailand stretching away to the south, with the Vietnamese island of Phu Quoc on the horizon, and the salt flats and rice fields of the plain below. The forest around the road is home to monkeys, hornbills and many other creatures, and in the early morning you might see gibbons swinging through the trees.

There is a ticket booth at the park entrance where foreigners pay a fee, and the road is busy at weekends and holidays with locals heading up for the views and the cooler air. The weather on the mountain can be very different from the coast: often cloudy, misty and cool, with sudden rain, so bring a jacket. There is fuel in Kampot, about fifteen kilometres away, but none on the climb itself, so fill up before you go. Ride carefully, as the curves can be deceptive and there are often cattle and monkeys on the road.
t.bokor mountain road point 3@10.6,104.0:
On top of Bokor the forest opens onto a wide, windswept plateau of scrub, rock and boggy grassland, and out of the mist appear the ghosts of a French hill station. The old Bokor Palace Hotel, opened in the 1920s, stands empty and blackened, its grand rooms open to the wind, and nearby a small Catholic church, also abandoned, sits on a rocky outcrop looking out over the sea. In the fog, which comes in fast and often, these buildings look like the set of a horror film, and indeed they have been used as one.

The hill station had a short and turbulent life. It was abandoned by the French in the 1940s, briefly revived in the 1960s as a resort for Cambodia's elite, and then fell into the hands of the Khmer Rouge, who held the mountain into the 1990s. Fighting took place around the hotel, and the plateau was heavily mined. It was cleared later, but it is still wise to stick to roads and paths. The ruins of a royal residence, known as the Black Palace, lie on the slopes nearby.

Today the plateau is also home to a large modern resort and casino, along with new buildings and roads, which has changed its character considerably. But there is still much to see: a huge statue of Lok Yeay Mao, a guardian spirit revered by Cambodians, stands near the road; the Wat Sampov Pram temple, named after rock formations said to resemble five boats, sits at the edge of the cliff with views over the coast; and Popokvil waterfall, a short walk from the road, is impressive in the rainy season.

The riding on the plateau is relaxed, with roads winding between the sights, often in thick fog, so use your lights and take care. There is little in the way of services, apart from the resort, which has restaurants and a fuel station, though it is wise to arrive with a full tank from Kampot. The air is cool, sometimes cold, and the weather changes in minutes, so bring a jacket and rain gear. Go up early or late in the day, when the low sun and drifting fog make the old buildings look their most haunted.
t.taltsy@52.0,104.6:
On the bank of the Angara, a little under halfway along the road from Irkutsk to Lake Baikal, stands a wooden tower that has travelled a long way. It was once part of the fort of Ilimsk, a seventeenth century Cossack outpost far to the north, and when the waters of a new reservoir threatened to drown the old fort in the Soviet era, the tower was dismantled, log by log, and rebuilt here. It is the centrepiece of Taltsy, an open-air museum of wooden architecture that brings together houses, barns, churches, mills and other buildings from villages across the Irkutsk region.

Wandering through the museum is like stepping back into Siberian village life of the nineteenth century. There are peasant houses with carved window frames, a small wooden church, a school, a blacksmith's forge and water mills, along with Buryat and Evenk dwellings that show how the native peoples of the region lived. Craftspeople sometimes demonstrate traditional skills, and there are festivals in summer and at Maslenitsa, the end-of-winter carnival. The setting, among birch and pine on a slope above the wide, clear Angara, is lovely in any season.

The road from Irkutsk to Listvyanka, sometimes called the Baikal Tract, is a pleasant ride, following the Angara through rolling forest with gentle bends and occasional views of the river. The surface is good, but the road is busy, especially on summer weekends when half of Irkutsk heads for the lake. Watch for speed traps and impatient drivers overtaking on blind bends. The best times are early morning or late afternoon, when the light on the river is soft and the traffic lighter.

The museum has a cafe and souvenir stalls, and entry costs a modest fee. Fuel and other services are available in Irkutsk and Listvyanka, about twenty-five kilometres further on. If you have time, try some of the local food, such as pozy, the steamed meat dumplings of the Buryats, or smoked omul, the famous fish of Baikal, which is sold in markets and stalls along the road. Allow an hour or two for the museum, then continue on toward the lake.
t.baikal shore@51.9,104.8:
Baikal holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet, in a rift so deep that its floor lies more than a kilometre below sea level. At this point near Listvyanka, where the Angara River leaves the lake as its only outflow, you can stand on the shore and look across a body of water so clear that stones are visible many metres down, and so cold that even in August a swim is a quick, gasping affair. In the middle of the river's source lies the Shaman Stone, a rock the Buryats held sacred and around which many legends are told.

The lake is ancient, around twenty-five million years old, and it has evolved its own world of life: hundreds of species found nowhere else, from the nerpa seal to translucent fish and sponges. The Baikal Museum in Listvyanka explains it all, with aquariums where you can watch the seals play. The village itself is a long strip of houses, hotels and cafes along the shore, busy and touristy in summer, with markets selling smoked omul, the lake's famous fish, and stalls of cedar nuts, berries and souvenirs.

As the finish of a ride along the Angara from Irkutsk, this is a fine end. The road follows the river through forest, then reaches the lake and runs along the shore into Listvyanka, with views across the water to the mountains of the Khamar-Daban range on the far side. The surface is good, though traffic is heavy in summer. A chairlift near the village climbs to a viewpoint named after the geologist Ivan Chersky, from which the view over the source of the Angara is magnificent, especially at sunset.

Listvyanka has fuel, shops, cafes and restaurants, and plenty of accommodation. Try the smoked omul, hot from the smokehouse, eaten with bread and a cold drink on the shore. In winter, the lake freezes solid and the ice becomes a highway for cars, skaters and walkers, with cracks, bubbles and blue hummocks that are mesmerising. At any season, watching the light play across the water here is the best way to end a day of riding.
t.near phra pradaeng@13.6,100.5:
This is the south-western edge of Bangkok, out where the city stops pretending to be a city and turns into a muddle of canals, warehouses, shrimp ponds and condo blocks on the Thonburi side of the Chao Phraya. Thung Khru and Bang Khun Thian are the districts on the map; Phra Pradaeng, the town that gives the label its name, lies across the river to the east. As a place to begin and end rides north to Ayutthaya or north-east to Khao Yai it makes practical sense, because you avoid crossing the dense middle of the capital twice a day.

Riding here is about patience and awareness rather than corners. Rama II Road, the main artery heading south-west, is wide, busy and lined with lorries, and the side sois are full of scooters doing whatever they like. Motorcycles are barred from the expressways and motorways in Thailand, so you will use the ordinary surface roads, where the leftmost lane is effectively the bike lane and buses swing into it without much notice. Leave before seven on a weekend and the whole city feels more relaxed; by mid-morning on a weekday it is a slow crawl in the heat.

There is more nature close by than you would guess. Bang Khun Thian is the only Bangkok district that touches the sea, a short strip of mangrove coast on the Gulf of Thailand where the city has tried to hold back erosion with bamboo fences and replanting. Across the river, Bang Krachao, the big loop of the Chao Phraya next to Phra Pradaeng, is known locally as Bangkok's green lung: orchards, raised walkways and quiet lanes kept largely free of development. It is a pleasant place to potter about on two wheels at the end of a long day, though the roads inside the loop are narrow and you will share them with cyclists.

Practically, this is ordinary suburban Bangkok, which means fuel stations, convenience stores and noodle stalls on almost every main road. The stores are a good place to buy cold water and electrolyte drinks before setting out. At the finish, after hours on the highway, a bowl of boat noodles at a canal-side shop and a slow ride home with the evening breeze off the river is about as civilised as Bangkok gets.
t.pattaya@12.9,100.9:
Sixty years ago Pattaya was a fishing village on a quiet bay south-east of Bangkok. Then, in the 1960s, American servicemen on leave from the Vietnam War started coming here for rest and recreation, and the place has never looked back. Today it is one of Thailand's biggest resorts, a city of high-rise hotels, condominium towers, shopping malls and a nightlife scene that is either legendary or notorious, depending on your perspective. It is loud, brash and busy, and for many riders it is a place to eat well, sleep and move on.

There is more to it than Walking Street, though. On the northern edge of the city, the Sanctuary of Truth is an extraordinary temple-like building made entirely of carved wood, still under construction after decades, standing by the sea like a vast, intricate sculpture. South of town, Jomtien Beach is calmer than the main bay, and boats leave for Ko Lan, an island with cleaner water and better beaches. Inland, a short ride takes you to the Silverlake vineyard area and to Khao Chi Chan, a cliff into which a giant golden image of the Buddha has been inlaid.

The food is excellent and varied, from street stalls selling grilled seafood and som tam to international restaurants of every kind. Prices range from very cheap to very expensive, and the choice is endless. Fuel is easy to find throughout the city and along Sukhumvit Road, the main highway running along the coast.

Riding in Pattaya demands patience and vigilance. The streets are crowded with cars, scooters and songthaews, the pick-up trucks used as shared taxis, which stop suddenly and without warning to pick up passengers. Traffic rules are loosely observed, and drunk drivers are a real risk at night. Outside the city, the roads inland towards the hills and lakes are quieter and more pleasant, with green countryside, fruit plantations and small villages. The coolest months, from November to February, are the best time to ride; the rest of the year is hot and often wet.
t.hua hin@12.6,100.0:
Thai royalty fell for the beach at Hua Hin long before anyone else, in the early twentieth century, when the new southern railway made it easy to reach from Bangkok. King Prajadhipok built a summer palace here in the 1920s and named it Klai Kangwon, which means Far from Worries. Thai kings have spent long periods here ever since, and the town has kept a slightly more refined, less frantic air than many other resorts.

The railway station is a symbol of the town: a small, ornate wooden building painted red and cream, with a royal waiting room that looks like a pavilion from a fairy tale. The beach stretches for kilometres south of the centre, with horses for hire and rows of seafood restaurants on stilts over the water. At the southern end, Khao Takiab, a rocky headland with a temple and a resident troop of monkeys, has fine views back along the coast.

Food is one of Hua Hin's great pleasures. The night market in the town centre is packed with stalls selling grilled seafood, noodles, fruit and desserts, and the seafood restaurants along the waterfront serve fresh crab, prawns and fish at reasonable prices. There are also plenty of cafés and international restaurants catering to the large community of foreign residents.

For riders, Hua Hin is a natural lunch stop and a good base for exploring further south. About an hour's ride away, Khao Sam Roi Yot National Park has limestone hills rising from marshes and mangroves, and the Phraya Nakhon cave, where a royal pavilion stands in a vast chamber lit by sunlight through a collapsed roof. The ride along the coast is pleasant, though Highway 4 is busy, so it is worth seeking out the smaller coastal roads. Fuel and services are easy to find. The cool season, from November to February, is the best time to visit, although even then the midday sun is strong, so start early.
t.samut songkhram@13.4,100.0:
Samut Songkhram is the smallest province in Thailand, a flat, watery land where the Mae Klong River meets the Gulf of Thailand, criss-crossed by canals and covered with coconut palms, orchards and salt pans. Its capital, also called Samut Songkhram or Mae Klong, is a busy market town about an hour and a half south-west of Bangkok, and it is home to one of the strangest sights in the country.

The Maeklong Railway Market runs along the railway line in the heart of the town. Vendors set out their vegetables, fish and fruit on the tracks themselves, under awnings that hang over the line. Several times a day, when a train approaches, a warning sounds, the awnings are pulled back, the goods closest to the rails are moved, and the train inches through the market, millimetres from the stalls. As soon as it has passed, everything goes back as it was. It is crowded, touristy and utterly fascinating.

A few kilometres upriver, Amphawa is famous for its floating market, held in the afternoons and evenings at weekends, when boats sell grilled seafood and sweets along the canal, and for the boat trips at night to see fireflies glittering in the trees along the river. King Rama II, a celebrated poet, was born in Amphawa, and a memorial park commemorates him. At the mouth of the river, Don Hoi Lot is a sandbank known for its razor clams, and the seafood restaurants nearby serve them fresh.

For riders, Samut Songkhram is a convenient fuel stop on the way to Kaeng Krachan and the forests of the west. The town has fuel stations, convenience stores and markets, and the local coconut sugar sweets make a good snack. The roads in the area are flat and generally straight, with heavy traffic on the main highways, especially Rama II Road from Bangkok. The smaller roads along the canals and through the orchards are quieter and more pleasant.

Somewhere north of Chiang Mai, on Route 1095 towards Pai and Mae Hong Son, a sign announces 1,864 curves, and riders queue to have their photo taken with it. That road, through the mountains of the far north-west, is the heart of the Mae Hong Son ride, and this point in Bangkok's western outskirts is where it all ends, back in the flatlands after the bikes have been flown or trucked home and the last kilometres ridden across the city.

The area around Thawi Watthana and Bang Yai is the old Thonburi orchard country, a district of canals, nurseries, fruit gardens and new housing estates, where the city is still in the process of swallowing the countryside. On weekends, the Taling Chan floating market, a few kilometres east, is a relaxed place to eat grilled fish and noodles on wooden platforms over the canal, with boats selling fruit and sweets alongside. It is much less touristy than the famous floating markets further out of town.

Bang Yai itself is a fast-growing suburb across the border in Nonthaburi province, with huge shopping malls, markets and a new metro line overhead, and it has every service you might need. Ending a ride here means you are close to the main roads north and west, but away from the dense traffic of central Bangkok.

The contrast with the north could hardly be greater. Up there, the roads twist through teak forests and mountain villages, with cool mornings, misty valleys and long climbs. Down here, it is flat, hot and humid, and the traffic is intense, especially in the evenings. Motorcycles are not permitted on the expressways and motorways, so stick to the surface roads, keep to the left lane and watch out for buses and pick-ups pulling in suddenly. Fuel and food are available on every main road. After weeks in the mountains, a bowl of boat noodles by a canal is a gentle way to readjust to the lowlands.
t.near bang pakong on the way back@13.6,10:
The Bang Pakong River reaches the Gulf of Thailand here in a wide, muddy estuary, fringed with mangroves, shrimp ponds and fishing villages, about an hour east of Bangkok. It is not a classic swimming spot, and it is honest to say so: the river water is brown with silt and the shore is mostly mud. The reason to stop is the estuary itself, and if you want a proper swim, the beach at Bang Saen, about twenty kilometres south in Chonburi, is the place most people from Bangkok head for, with a long sandy shore, shady trees and stalls selling seafood.

The estuary has a surprising resident. Irrawaddy dolphins, a small, round-headed species found in coastal waters and rivers of South-East Asia, live around the river mouth, and local boat operators offer trips to see them, especially in the cooler months. Spotting their grey backs rolling in the brown water is a quiet thrill. The mangroves are also full of birds, from egrets and herons to kingfishers.

Upstream, the river flows past Chachoengsao, a provincial capital known for Wat Sothon Wararam, a huge white temple housing a revered Buddha image that draws pilgrims from all over Thailand. The countryside around is flat and green, with rice paddies, fish ponds and orchards.

On the way back to Bangkok, the main road is Highway 34, the Bang Na–Trat road, a wide, busy route lined with factories and warehouses, with heavy truck traffic. It is not a pleasant ride, but it is direct. The smaller roads along the coast and through the villages are slower but more interesting. Fuel, convenience stores and seafood restaurants are easy to find along the way. Riverside restaurants serve grilled prawns, crab and fish, and eating them by the water as the sun goes down, before the final push back into the city, is a good reward.

Khlong Luang sprawls across the flat rice plain north of Bangkok, a district of canals, industrial estates and university campuses. Thammasat University's Rangsit campus, the Asian Institute of Technology and Thailand Science Park are all here, along with Navanakorn, one of the country's large industrial zones. It is a busy, modern place that gives little hint of the countryside it once was.

The canals are the key to its history. In the late nineteenth century, under King Chulalongkorn, a grid of canals known as the Rangsit system was dug across these marshy plains to irrigate rice fields and open them to settlement. Khlong Luang means the great canal, and the waterways still define the landscape, with houses on stilts, small boats and lotus ponds between the factories and shopping malls.

Riding here is about navigating traffic. Phahonyothin Road, Highway 1, runs north towards Ayutthaya and beyond, busy with trucks, buses and countless motorcycles. Expect heat, humidity and sudden downpours in the rainy season, from roughly June to October. Watch for vehicles entering from side roads and U-turn points.

t.nakhon pathom@13.8,100.1:
The great golden-orange dome of Phra Pathom Chedi towers over Nakhon Pathom, and at over a hundred metres tall it is one of the largest stupas in the world. Tradition holds that Buddhism first reached the region here, more than a thousand years ago, when this was a centre of the Dvaravati culture, and the original, much smaller stupa was later encased in the present structure in the nineteenth century by King Mongkut, who had seen the ruins as a monk. Walking around its base, with its galleries, shrines and bells, is an experience not to miss.

Nakhon Pathom is a busy provincial city west of Bangkok, surrounded by rice fields, orchards and canals. King Vajiravudh built the Sanam Chandra Palace here in the early twentieth century, a curious mix of Thai and European styles, set in a large park. The city is also known for its food, particularly its sticky rice cooked in bamboo tubes, khao lam, and its pomelos, grown in the orchards around the city.

The riding here is about getting through traffic. The roads are flat, busy and full of trucks, buses and motorcycles, and the heat can be intense. The main highways to Bangkok and to Kanchanaburi are fast but chaotic, and the minor roads through the countryside are quieter but can be narrow and rough. In the rainy season, sudden downpours can flood the roads.

Nakhon Pathom has plenty of fuel stations, markets and restaurants, and the market around the chedi is a great place to eat. Try the khao lam, a sweet treat of sticky rice, coconut milk and beans. Ayutthaya, the old capital, lies to the north, a pleasant ride along the river.
t.near krathum baen@13.6,100.3:
Krathum Baen is a district of Samut Sakhon province, south-west of Bangkok, where the city's sprawl meets factories, shrimp farms and the last of the old orchards. The Tha Chin River, a distributary of the Chao Phraya, flows past on its way to the Gulf of Thailand, and the land is crossed by canals that once carried produce to market by boat. It is a working area, busy with trucks and commuters, and a place most riders pass through on their way to somewhere else.

Samut Sakhon, the provincial capital at the mouth of the Tha Chin, is famous for its seafood market, one of the largest in Thailand, and for the salt pans along the coast, where salt is still harvested by hand in the dry season. The Rama II Road, Highway 35, runs south from Bangkok through the province towards the beaches of the western gulf and the south of the country, and it is one of the busiest roads in Thailand.

There is no real high ground on the Tha Chin plain west of Krathum Baen; the land is as flat as a table, built from river silt over millennia. What passes for height here is the hump of a bridge over the river or a canal, and from such a vantage the view is of water, palms, temple roofs and the occasional factory chimney. The river curves lazily through the landscape, and long-tail boats still ply its brown waters.

The area straddles the border between Samut Sakhon and Nakhon Pathom provinces, and it is a mix of old and new. Pathum Thani means city of lotuses, a name said to have been given by King Rama II when the local people presented him with lotus flowers during a visit. The province, just north of Bangkok on the Chao Phraya, was settled by Mon refugees from Burma in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and their culture survives in temples, festivals and food along the river. Wat Chedi Hoi, a temple decorated with millions of ancient fossil shells, is one of the area's curiosities.

Today, the province is a mix of suburbs, industrial estates and rice fields, with the Chao Phraya flowing broad and brown through its heart. The river is lined with temples, houses on stilts and riverside restaurants, and boats still carry goods and passengers. The canals that cross the land were dug in the nineteenth century to irrigate rice fields, and some of them are still used by farmers and fishermen.

The riding here is about navigating traffic and heat. The main roads are busy, with trucks, buses and countless motorcycles, and the heat can be intense. Motorcycles are not allowed on the expressways, so you will be on the main roads. The minor roads along the river are quieter and more scenic, but they can be narrow and rough. In the rainy season, floods can be a problem; the great flood of 2011 left much of the province under water for weeks.

Pathum Thani has plenty of fuel stations, markets and restaurants. A meal at a riverside restaurant, with grilled fish and spicy salads, is a good way to break the journey. The road north towards Mae Hong Son is long, and the mountains are still far away.
t.garachico@28.4,-16.8:
Garachico looks like a peaceful seaside town, and it is, but it is also a place that was nearly erased. In 1706 a volcanic eruption sent lava down the slopes behind the town and into the sea, filling the harbour that had made Garachico one of the main ports on Tenerife. The ships that used to sail from here now belong to the history books, and the town's fortunes shifted. What remains is a handsome settlement of old houses, a small fortress by the water, and a sea-edge where black lava has been shaped into natural swimming pools that locals still use.

You reach it by roads that come down from the highlands in curves and switchbacks, often with banana plantations and steep terraced farms on either side. About 6,000 people live in the municipality, which means fuel and food are not a problem, and the bigger centres of Icod de los Vinos and Los Silos are just a few kilometres away along the coast. Icod is famous for its enormous ancient dragon tree, which is worth a look if you have the time.

The riding in this north-western corner of Tenerife is some of the best on the island. The road toward Masca and the interior twists through narrow valleys, with hairpins that need respect and passing places that need patience, because tour buses and rental cars share the width. Early morning is the answer, before the traffic builds and while the light picks out the ravines. Weather is changeable: the north side catches cloud, and you can ride from sun at the coast into mist in the pines above, so a light jacket in the bag is sensible.

For something to eat, the seafront has a number of simple places serving fresh fish and the island's wrinkled potatoes with a red or green mojo sauce, and the local wines are worth trying in the evening. Park the bike near the old quarter, walk the cobbled streets under balconies, and look at the lava where the harbour used to be. It gives you a sense of scale that no viewpoint can.
t.mogan@27.9,-15.7:
Mogán is the inland village that gives the south-west of Gran Canaria its name, and it is a good example of how this island works: a sunny, busy coast, and just behind it a mountain world that feels like another country. The village sits some distance up a barranco, one of the deep, dry ravines that fan out from the central peaks to the sea. The better-known place is the harbour town of Puerto de Mogán on the coast, with its canals and bougainvillea, but the older settlement up the valley has a quieter pace and a more rural feel.

The municipality has around 21,000 people, spread between the resorts and the hills, and Puerto Rico is the larger neighbour down the coast. There is fuel and food in the area, and the road into the valley is one you will want to ride at a deliberate speed. It climbs in bends that tighten and widen as the valley narrows, with the rock walls turning from ochre to rust and the vegetation changing from sun-baked scrub to patches of palms, fruit trees and little farms. In the valleys here you will see mango, avocado and papaya growing where water allows.

Gran Canaria is sometimes called a continent in miniature, and the claim has some truth: the island is a volcanic cone, and the weather varies sharply with altitude and side. The south-west is dry and warm for much of the year, but once you climb toward the central highlands the temperature drops and mist can roll over the ridges. This makes spring and autumn the best seasons, when the heat is moderate and the light is clear. Midsummer afternoons can be hot, and the winter north is cloudier.

Take care with surfaces. Mountain roads here are narrow, occasionally rough, and shared with cyclists, goats and hire cars driven by people still learning the width of the car. Watch for gravel on the inside of bends after rain, and for rockfall on the steeper cuttings. Stop in the village for a coffee, look up at the barranco walls, and take note of how quickly the road drops back toward the sea afterwards.
t.agaete@28.1,-15.7:
Agaete sits at the north-west tip of Gran Canaria, where the mountains drop abruptly toward the Atlantic, and it has the feel of a place that has seen a lot of arrivals. The town itself is white-walled and low, set a little back from the water, while the old fishing harbour of Puerto de las Nieves lies on the coast with a ferry terminal and a row of seafood restaurants. From there ferries cross to Tenerife, and on a clear day Mount Teide stands up on the horizon like a cut-out.

Beside the harbour rises a thin sea stack called the Dedo de Dios, the Finger of God. Its tip was broken off in a tropical storm in 2005, and the stump still stands as a local landmark. The valley behind the town is a surprise: it is green and sheltered, with fruit trees and, unusually for Europe, coffee plantations, which benefit from the mild climate on this side of the island. Above the valley the pine forest of Tamadaba climbs toward high ridges and vertiginous drops to the sea.

About 5,500 people live in Agaete itself, with the larger towns of Gáldar and Guía a few kilometres east, so fuel, groceries and a proper meal are all easy to find. The riding is in the roads leading up and away. Inland and upward, the route to Tamadaba and to the mountain villages involves tight, climbing bends with sharp exposure, and the west-coast road southward is famously winding, with big cliffs and sections that can be affected by rockfall, so it pays to check conditions before you commit.

Choose your timing with the wind and the sun in mind. Mornings are usually clear and calm, afternoons can bring cloud to the heights, and the trade winds make some exposed sections gusty. After the ride, grab a table near the harbour, order whatever came off the boat that day with a plate of local potatoes, and sit watching the ferry come and go while the stack turns pink in the last light. It is an easy place to stay longer than you meant.

Samut Sakhon smells of the sea. The city sits at the mouth of the Tha Chin River where it flows into the Gulf of Thailand, about thirty kilometres southwest of Bangkok, and it has been a fishing port for centuries. Locals often still call it Mahachai, its old name. Boats crowd the river, and the fish market near the pier is one of the busiest in the country, piled with prawns, squid, crabs and fish of every kind.

Around the city, the flat coastal land is crisscrossed by canals and dotted with salt pans and shrimp farms. Along the road to the west you can see workers raking salt into white heaps in the evaporation ponds, a tradition that goes back generations. Samut Sakhon also has a large community of migrant workers from Myanmar, many working in the seafood processing industry, and their presence gives parts of the city a distinctive character, with Burmese shops and food.

One of the most unusual ways to arrive is by train. The Maeklong Railway runs from Bangkok to Mahachai, where passengers take a ferry across the river and then another train continues to the famous market at Maeklong, where vendors pull back their awnings as the train passes through the stalls.

About the swim: the coast here is mud flats and mangroves rather than beaches, and the water is brown, shallow and used by fishing boats. Not a place for swimming. If you want a beach, the resorts of Hua Hin or Pattaya are a long ride away. Here, the best way to cool off is a cold drink at a seafood restaurant overlooking the river or the sea.

Riding in Samut Sakhon is busy and flat. The Rama II Road, the main highway southwest from Bangkok, is crowded with trucks and buses, and the city streets are full of scooters, pickups and street vendors. Traffic can be chaotic, with sudden lane changes and vehicles entering without warning. Fuel and food are everywhere. Try the seafood, especially grilled prawns, steamed crabs and fried fish, at one of the many restaurants by the water, then head back toward Ayutthaya and the river roads.
